bib.title: Support-Vector Machines and Kernel Methods (Chapter 19 of Computer Age Statistical Inference)

question: How do support-vector machines build a classifier directly via margins, how does the kernel trick extend them to nonlinear boundaries, and how does this relate to logistic regression, RKHS function fitting and kernel smoothing?

limits: No benchmark beyond two small examples (leukemia, one protein set); single runs, no error bars.
Quadratic penalty means all features are in the model, so no sparsity unless the lasso penalty is swapped in.
Kernel SVMs and kernel smoothing suffer the curse of dimensionality; neighbourhoods stop being local in high dimensions.
Overfit risk: small budget B with radial kernel makes islands (Fig 19.6 right).
Kernel smoothing is memory-based: all training data kept, local fit recomputed per prediction.
Polynomial kernels are 'mainly useful as existence proofs'.
Chapter is dated 2016; no deep learning comparison.
practices: Tune the margin budget B (equivalently lambda) by cross-validation; larger B gives more support points, more stability and lower variance (Sec 19.2).
Use soft margin even for separable data to regularise (Sec 19.2).
For wide data (p>>n) where logistic regression fails on separable data, use an optimal separating hyperplane (Sec 19.1).
Swap ridge for lasso penalty for sparse linear support-vector classifiers, e.g. R package liblineaR (Sec 19.3).
Use radial kernel as the usual practical choice; polynomial kernels are mostly existence proofs (Sec 19.4).
Prefer SVM over logistic regression for separable data because of normalisation; prefer logistic regression for overlapped classes since it targets the class probability logit (note 5).
Choose kernel width/span by cross-validation; use local linear regression rather than Nadaraya-Watson to remove boundary bias (Sec 19.8).
Any similarity that behaves like an inner product (positive semidefinite) can define a kernel for non-vector objects such as strings (Sec 19.5, 19.6).

terms.definition: the linear classifier that creates the largest margin between the two classes (also known as an optimal-margin classifier)
S in beta-hat = sum over S of alpha-hat_i x_i; points on the margin (plus violators in the soft margin)
allows margin violations xi_i with total budget B (sum xi_i <= B)
L_H(y,f(x)) = [1 - y f(x)]_+, applied to the margin y f(x); zero for margin above 1
solution depends on data only through inner products, so K(x,z)=<h(x),h(z)> gives fits in an enlarged feature space at no extra cost
K(x,z)=exp(-gamma ||x-z||^2) (minus sign unconfirmed in text layer), positive definite, infinite-dimensional feature space
n x n matrix of pairwise inner products (X X' in linear case, K in general)
space H_K of functions spanned by K(., z) with norm ||f||_HK acting as roughness measure
kernel-weighted average sum y_i K(x0,xi) / sum K(x0,xi)
K_s = (1-u^3)^3 if u<=1 else 0, u_i=d_i/d_(m), span s=m/n
at each x0 solve kernel-weighted least squares; fitted value removes boundary bias to first order
no fitted model; all training data saved and local fit recomputed per prediction
